A friend of mine is moving out soon, and he isn't sure whether his parents have legal ownership of some of his things. His parents aren't happy about him moving, so they're trying to keep as much of his stuff as they can to try and keep him in. Here's what we want to know:

a) Does he have legal ownership of birthday/friendly gifts given to him by non-family when he was a minor? He is currently 20.

b) Does he have legal ownership of birthday/friendly gifts given to him by family when he was a minor?

c) Does he have legal ownership of things like, for example, toothbrush and clothing, that were not purchased for a birthday or special occasion, but were bought specifically for him by parents?

d) Anything else I might have missed.

Any help would be appreciated. Please cite laws if you can, I want to have something to cite his parents to if they object.
[Florida] Do I legally own gifts given to me?

If they were truly gifts, then they are his to do with as he pleases: http://legal-dictionary.thefreedictionary.com/gift

Gift given by people other than family are his and he can do with them as he pleases. As far as the other stuff; A toothbrush he used is his, as there is no expectation that it would be returned. His bed, on the other hand, is likely NOT considered a gift, even though he has been using it exclusively for some time. Clothing, and other "gifts" are likely things a court will not contest as his.

According to this site - http://legal-dictionary.thefreedictionary.com/Legal+Rights+of+Children - Children do have the right to own and acquire property.
I'll cite these for now, but I'll probably need to cite laws sooner or later. Thanks a lot for the response.
Why even go that far? - If they are that adamant about material things, and using them as a way to get him to comply, then it is far better to simply let them go - the parents and the material items.

He owns almost literally nothing if his parents are right (I've found they aren't). He has to start from scratch. That means his work-from-home job would be done on a library computer because even his computer was a gift from them. If they lay claim on gifts given to him, he can't even work independently (on top of the fact that most of his hobbies are based on the computer). This is a huge relief for him.

Gifts during the donor's life are called inter vivos gifts (as opposed to testamentary gifts given through a will). Inter vivos gifts are irrevocable if the following 3 criteria are met:

  1. Donative intent (the giver intended to make a gift instead of a loan or borrow situation),
  2. Delivery (of the thing to the recipient), and
  3. Acceptance (of the gift).

If these conditions are met, the legal title for the property (yes, even a toothbrush has "title" in a legal context) has passed to the recipient and the giver can't change his mind - no take-backs! The elements for an inter vivos gift in Florida can be found at Mulato v. Mulato, 705 So. 2d 57, 62 (Fla. 4th DCA 1997) recently affirmed in Welch v. Dececco (Fla. 5th DCA 2012).

To restate, if the giver meant to give a gift, delivered the property, and the recipient accepted it, the gift is complete. Your friend gets to keep it.

Probably the biggest argument your going to get is that "I never intended to give that to you." If true, no intent to give = no gift, but cross that bridge when it comes. I think proving that the television you gave your 16 year-old 6 years ago wasn't a gift would be well-nigh impossible so I wouldn't sweat that one too much. Oh, and the minor thing doesn't matter. Once you're 18 you now hold legal title to all your stuff, including your toothbrush. Hope this helps.

You will find that statutes cover only part of the law, and even a statute can be contested. Case law is the primary reference for presenting a legal argument, and is known as the principle of stare decisis, meaning that courts must follow the decisions of higher level courts within the same jurisdiction. So in a lot of situations, people are looking for case law, not a statute.
